title: Shaken, Not Stirred — In Hindi: Shekhar Kapur Backs John Abraham as the Next James Bond
excerpt: The director who launched Daniel Craig's career says John Abraham 'has the Bond charm' — and the franchise's biggest-ever casting search makes an Indian 007 less fantasy than you'd think
body:
It started with a tweet. Shekhar Kapur — the director who gave the world *Elizabeth*, *Bandit Queen*, and *Mr. India* — posted a photo of John Abraham with a caption that sent Bollywood Twitter into meltdown: "He has the Bond charm. Shaken not stirred."

The internet did what the internet does. Within hours, #JohnAbrahamBond was trending, fan edits flooded Instagram, and the man himself responded with the kind of line that actually does sound like something 007 would say: "I'll happily start practising my martini order immediately."

## Why This Isn't Just Another Internet Fantasy

Here's the thing about Shekhar Kapur's endorsement that separates it from the usual "Which Bollywood actor should play Bond?" listicle: Kapur is the director who *actually launched Daniel Craig's career*. Craig appeared in Kapur's 1998 film *Elizabeth* in a small role, and Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson have said they noticed Craig partly through that performance. When Shekhar Kapur says someone has Bond energy, the franchise's decision-makers have historically listened.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DYZrhj1lhB8/

John Abraham, for his part, isn't a random Bollywood hunk being thrust into a fantasy casting. The 53-year-old has spent the last decade building an action-hero brand — *Pathaan* (where he squared off against Shah Rukh Khan), the *Dhoom* franchise, *Attack*, *Tehran* — that's closer to the Bond ethos than almost any other Indian actor working today. He has the physicality, the brooding intensity, and crucially, the kind of screen presence that doesn't need dialogue to fill a room.

## The Bigger Conversation: Desi Representation at the Top Table

The Bond casting conversation has always been a proxy war for bigger questions about representation in global entertainment. When Idris Elba was rumoured for the role, it sparked debates about race and tradition. When Henry Cavill and Aaron Taylor-Johnson were mentioned, it was about age and brand. Now, the question is: could an Indian actor actually wear the tuxedo?

The franchise is at a crossroads. Amazon MGM Studios completed its acquisition of the Bond franchise, Denis Villeneuve has been tapped to direct the next film, and auditions are reportedly underway. The search for Craig's successor has been going on for over four years — longer than any previous transition in the franchise's 60-year history.

An Indian Bond would be seismic. Not just for Bollywood's global ambitions, but for the millions of South Asian viewers who've grown up watching Bond films and never seen anyone who looks like them in the driver's seat of that Aston Martin.

## The Fan Debate: Abraham vs. Rampal vs. Reality

Social media hasn't been uniformly convinced. "No bro, if you're going Indian, it would be Arjun Rampal," one viral reply argued, citing Rampal's sharper jawline and more classically Western features. Others pointed to younger actors like Siddhant Chaturvedi or even the ever-suave Hrithik Roshan as better fits.

But Abraham's supporters have a compelling counter: Bond isn't just about looks. Craig proved that Bond could be blunt, bruised, and emotionally vulnerable. Abraham's best performances — *Madras Cafe*, *Batla House*, *Romeo Akbar Walter* — show a similar range: a man of action who carries genuine weight behind his eyes.

## What Would an Indian Bond Mean for the Diaspora?

For South Asians in the West, the very fact that this conversation is happening — seriously, not as a joke — represents a tectonic shift. Twenty years ago, the idea of an Indian James Bond would have been dismissed as absurd. Today, with Indian cinema crossing Rs 1,800-crore box offices (*Dhurandhar 2*), Indian actors headlining Hollywood projects, and Indian culture reshaping global entertainment from music to fashion, the conversation feels less like fantasy and more like inevitability.

John Abraham may or may not be the next James Bond. But the fact that a director with direct ties to the franchise is putting an Indian actor's name in the ring? That alone is a martini worth raising.

Shaken, not stirred. Obviously.
